raw_evidence.label: Origin: Randall Munroe's 2010 xkcd Color Survey
raw_evidence.content: In April 2010, Randall Munroe — author of the webcomic xkcd — launched a web-based color naming survey. Visitors were shown a colored square (drawn from the sRGB monitor gamut) and asked, in plain text, to type whatever name came to mind. Over the course of about a month the survey collected roughly 222,500 user sessions and more than five million individual color-naming responses, making it one of the largest crowdsourced color-naming experiments ever conducted. After cleaning out spam, joke entries (including some attempted SQL injections), and gibberish, Munroe published a list of the 954 RGB monitor colors that received consistent, recognizable names — a dataset that subsequently became canonical in design tools, scientific Python (matplotlib's `xkcd:` color namespace), and R packages.

sources.title: Color Survey Results — xkcd
facts: Survey collected over 5 million colors named across 222,500 user sessions
954 colors with consistent named identifications were published
Some respondents attempted SQL injection attacks
Indigo was artificially included to make ROY G. BIV work

raw_evidence.label: Dataset shape and what one row means
raw_evidence.content: The TidyTuesday release breaks the survey into three CSVs. `color_ranks.csv` (954 rows) is the canonical published list — each row a named color with its rank and hex code. `users.csv` (~152k rows) records demographic data per user: monitor type, Y-chromosome flag, colorblindness flag, and a precomputed spam probability. `answers.csv` (over 1 million rows) is a filtered subset of all the raw responses: only those answers where the typed name was one of the top-5 ranked names for the displayed color. Each answer row gives user_id, the hex code shown, and the rank (1–5) of the name they gave. This filtering matters: it pre-selects for 'reasonable' answers, so this dataset is best for measuring agreement among the ranked names rather than open-ended naming variety.

raw_evidence.label: Dataset shape
raw_evidence.content: The TidyTuesday release contains three CSVs: color_ranks (949 rows × 3 cols — note: 949 actually published, not the round 954 sometimes quoted), users (152,401 rows × 5 cols of demographic and quality flags), and answers (1,058,211 rows × 3 cols). Each answer row records one user being shown one hex code and typing one of the top-5 color names — so this dataset is a filtered subset of the original ~5 million-response survey, retaining only those entries where the typed name was 'purple', 'green', 'blue', 'pink', or 'brown'.

# --- ana_01: Dataset shape ---

users = pd.read_csv(f'{DATA_DIR}/users.csv')
# answers is large — use chunked count first
answers_n = sum(1 for _ in open(f'{DATA_DIR}/answers.csv')) - 1
print(f"color_ranks rows: {len(color_ranks)}, cols: {len(color_ranks.columns)}")
print(f"users rows: {len(users)}, cols: {len(users.columns)}")
print(f"answers rows (line count): {answers_n}")
raw_evidence.output:
color_ranks rows: 949, cols: 3
users rows: 152401, cols: 5
answers rows (line count): 1058211

Source: Linguistic relativity and the color naming debate — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_relativity_and_the_color_naming_debate) Facts: Russian speakers distinguish light and dark blue faster due to separate basic terms; Berlin & Kay supported a universalist account; later work documented relativist effects

raw_evidence.label: Why color naming is scientifically interesting
raw_evidence.content: Color is the textbook case for the Sapir-Whorf debate: does the language we speak shape how we perceive the world? Berlin and Kay's universalist account argued that color cognition is largely culture-independent. raw_evidence.label: Where each name lives in HSV space — centroids
raw_evidence.content: Median hue, saturation and value for each top-5 name carve out near-non-overlapping wedges of HSV space. Brown sits low and dim: median hue 31°, saturation 0.71, value 0.54 (i.e. dark orange-brown). Green is at hue 117°, S 0.78, V 0.75. Blue is at hue 223°, S 0.80, V 0.81. Purple at hue 284°, S 0.73, V 0.72. Pink at hue 323°, S 0.61, V 0.92 — uniquely bright and pastel. The mean and median nearly coincide for all colors except pink, which has bimodality from the ~0°/360° wrap-around.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_11 ===")
centroids = df.groupby('answer_name').agg(
    n=('hex_lower','size'),
    H_med=('H','median'), S_med=('S','median'), V_med=('V','median'),
    H_mean=('H','mean'),  S_mean=('S','mean'),  V_mean=('V','mean'),
).reset_index()
print(centroids.to_string(index=False))
centroids.to_csv('/tmp/centroids.csv', index=False)

raw_evidence.label: Hue ranges (5th–95th percentile) per top-5 name
raw_evidence.content: The 5th-to-95th-percentile hue range covers each name's working territory. Brown spans hues 8–91° (a wide warm wedge), green 74–158°, blue 178–257°, purple 252–327°, and pink 15–352° (because pink wraps around the 0°/360° boundary). Adjacent names overlap slightly at boundaries: brown→green at ~75°, green→blue at ~160°, blue→purple at ~255°, purple→pink at ~325°, pink→brown at ~15°. These boundary regions are where naming disagreement is highest in subsequent analyses.
raw_evidence.code:
range_data = []
for name in TOP5.values():
    sub = df[df['answer_name']==name]
    h = sub['H'].values
    if len(h)==0: continue
    p5, p95 = np.percentile(h, [5,95])
    md = np.median(h)
    print(f"  {name}: hue {p5:.0f}–{p95:.0f}° (median {md:.0f}°), n={len(sub):,}")
    range_data.append({'name':name, 'p5':p5, 'p95':p95, 'median':md, 'n':len(sub)})

green: hue 74-158 (median 117)

brown: hue 8-91 (median 31)

raw_evidence.content: Binning displayed hex into a 12×12×12 RGB cube (1,728 cells, 612 answers per cell on average) and looking at the most-popular name per cell: 1,063 of 1,606 well-sampled cells (66.2%) have a winner with ≥90% share. 849 (52.9%) are at ≥95%. Only 14 cells (0.9%) drop below 50% winner share, and just 3 below 40%. The mean winner share across cells is 88.6%, median 95.8%. Color naming, in this top-5 vocabulary, is overwhelmingly *settled* across most of the RGB cube — the boundary regions are narrow.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_13 ===")
cell_counts = df.groupby('cell').size()
print(f"Non-empty cells (of {NB**3} possible): {len(cell_counts)}")
print(f"Cells with n>=50: {(cell_counts>=50).sum()}")
print(f"Cells with n>=200: {(cell_counts>=200).sum()}")
print(f"Mean answers per non-empty cell: {cell_counts.mean():.1f}, median: {cell_counts.median():.0f}")

# Aggregate per cell: name distribution
cell_grp = df.groupby(['cell','answer_name']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
cell_grp['n'] = cell_grp.sum(axis=1)
for name in TOP5.values():
    if name not in cell_grp.columns:
        cell_grp[name] = 0
cell_grp['winner'] = cell_grp[list(TOP5.values())].idxmax(axis=1)
cell_grp['winner_pct'] = cell_grp[list(TOP5.values())].max(axis=1) / cell_grp['n']
cell_grp = cell_grp.reset_index()

# Cell coordinates: average RGB of cell center
def cell_to_rgb(c):
    r=c//(NB*NB); g=(c%(NB*NB))//NB; b=c%NB
    return (r+0.5)*256/NB, (g+0.5)*256/NB, (b+0.5)*256/NB
cell_rgb = np.array([cell_to_rgb(c) for c in cell_grp['cell']])
cell_grp['cR']=cell_rgb[:,0]; cell_grp['cG']=cell_rgb[:,1]; cell_grp['cB']=cell_rgb[:,2]

# Restrict to well-sampled cells
ws = cell_grp[cell_grp['n']>=50].copy()
print(f"\nWell-sampled cells (n>=50): {len(ws)}")
print("Winner-name distribution across well-sampled cells:")
print(ws['winner'].value_counts())
print(f"\nMean winner share: {ws['winner_pct'].mean()*100:.2f}%")
print(f"Median winner share: {ws['winner_pct'].median()*100:.2f}%")
print(f"Cells with winner_pct >= 0.95: {(ws['winner_pct']>=0.95).sum()}")
print(f"Cells with winner_pct >= 0.90: {(ws['winner_pct']>=0.90).sum()}")
print(f"Cells with winner_pct < 0.50: {(ws['winner_pct']<0.50).sum()}")
print(f"Cells with winner_pct < 0.40: {(ws['winner_pct']<0.40).sum()}")

    print(f"\nMost canonically '{name}' cells (highest winner_pct):")
    print(pure[['center_hex','n','winner_pct',name]].to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: The fuchsia/magenta line — pink-purple boundary
raw_evidence.content: The hue range 290–340° is where 'pink' and 'purple' contend for naming territory. At hue 280° purple owns 95.4%; at 300° purple still leads (88.2%) but pink jumps to 11.0%. raw_evidence.label: Chromosomal sex and color vision
raw_evidence.content: The dataset records, per user, whether they self-reported having a Y chromosome (a proxy for chromosomal sex) and whether they reported being colorblind. This framing — using chromosomes rather than gender — was deliberate: red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive, so individuals with one X chromosome (XY) are far more likely to be colorblind than those with two (XX). Population estimates put red-green color vision deficiency at about 8% of XY individuals versus 0.5% of XX individuals — roughly a 16x difference. Beyond physiology, the World Color Survey and follow-up linguistic research have documented that women use significantly more elaborate non-basic color terms (mauve, chartreuse, beige) and make finer green/blue distinctions, while men more often use the merged 'grue' category. The xkcd data is a chance to measure both effects in a single English-speaking online sample.

raw_evidence.label: The crude-name effect and joke responses
raw_evidence.content: Munroe's much-quoted finding was that the 'most masculine' (most disproportionately popular among XY respondents) color names were dominated by joke or crude entries: 'penis', 'gay', 'WTF', 'dunno', and the misspelling 'baige'. The most feminine entries by contrast were aesthetic descriptors: dusty teal, blush pink, dusty lavender, butter yellow, dusky rose. He commented 'I weep for my gender'. This is itself a finding about online survey behavior — male respondents' tendency to submit nonsense or transgressive entries — but it is also a measurement issue, because spam-flagged users overlap heavily with this population.

The largest cell-level XY-vs-XX divergence (0.378) is at #203535 — a dark teal-grey — where 68% of XY users said 'green' but 65% of XX said 'blue'. Other strongly-divergent cells are pink/purple/brown borderlands (#b50a4a, #e0b58a, #b5a0a0) where XX users converge harder on a single name while XY users spread answers more evenly. The pattern is consistent with prior linguistic research: XX users use color terms with higher in-group agreement at the same boundaries.

raw_evidence.label: Chromosomal sex and color vision
raw_evidence.content: The dataset records, per user, whether they self-reported having a Y chromosome (a proxy for chromosomal sex) and whether they reported being colorblind. This framing — using chromosomes rather than gender — was deliberate: red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive, so individuals with one X chromosome (XY) are far more likely to be colorblind than those with two (XX). Population estimates put red-green color vision deficiency at about 8% of XY individuals versus 0.5% of XX individuals — roughly a 16x difference. Beyond physiology, the World Color Survey and follow-up linguistic research have documented that women use significantly more elaborate non-basic color terms (mauve, chartreuse, beige) and make finer green/blue distinctions, while men more often use the merged 'grue' category. The xkcd data is a chance to measure both effects in a single English-speaking online sample.

raw_evidence.label: Spam probability is concentrated and skewed XY

The xkcd data is a chance to measure both effects in a single English-speaking online sample.

raw_evidence.label: The crude-name effect and joke responses
raw_evidence.content: Munroe's much-quoted finding was that the 'most masculine' (most disproportionately popular among XY respondents) color names were dominated by joke or crude entries: 'penis', 'gay', 'WTF', 'dunno', and the misspelling 'baige'. The most feminine entries by contrast were aesthetic descriptors: dusty teal, blush pink, dusty lavender, butter yellow, dusky rose. He commented 'I weep for my gender'. This is itself a finding about online survey behavior — male respondents' tendency to submit nonsense or transgressive entries — but it is also a measurement issue, because spam-flagged users overlap heavily with this population.

raw_evidence.label: Spam probability is concentrated and skewed XY
raw_evidence.content: Mean spam_prob is 0.218 for XY users vs 0.162 for XX, despite identical medians (0.030). The high tail is the asymmetry: 7.40% of XY users have spam_prob > 0.5 vs 4.59% of XX. Within high-spam buckets the XY share rises dramatically — among spam_prob > 0.75, 81.5% of users are XY (vs the baseline ~71% XY share). Among spam_prob 0.5–0.75, 79.2% are XY. This empirically validates Munroe's 2010 anecdote that crude/joke entries skewed male. It also means any chromosome-conditional naming finding must include spam filtering as a robustness check.

raw_evidence.label: Colorblind users disagree on naming much more than non-colorblind
raw_evidence.content: The cell-level mean Manhattan-divergence between colorblind and non-colorblind answer distributions is 0.117 (median 0.065) — almost three times the chromosome divergence (0.040). Aggregate: colorblind users say 'green' 32.16% (vs 29.55% for non-colorblind, +2.62 pp), 'pink' 15.60% (vs 12.24%, +3.36 pp), 'purple' just 17.99% (vs 23.93%, -5.94 pp). The biggest cell-level divergence is at #b5a0ca (a soft lilac): colorblind users called it 'pink' 56.5% of the time while non-colorblind users called it 'purple' 87.4%. The pattern is consistent with red-green color blindness compressing the perceptual distance between purple and pink (both with red-channel components) — colorblind users substitute 'pink' where non-colorblind see 'purple'.

print("=== ana_20 ===")
cell_cb = clean[clean['colorblind']==1].groupby(['cell','answer_name']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
cell_ncb = clean[clean['colorblind']==0].groupby(['cell','answer_name']).size().unstack(fill_value=0)
for name in TOP5.values():
    if name not in cell_cb.columns: cell_cb[name]=0
    if name not in cell_ncb.columns: cell_ncb[name]=0
cell_cb['n_cb']=cell_cb[list(TOP5.values())].sum(axis=1)
cell_ncb['n_ncb']=cell_ncb[list(TOP5.values())].sum(axis=1)
cbm = cell_cb.join(cell_ncb, lsuffix='_cb', rsuffix='_ncb', how='inner').reset_index()
cbm = cbm[(cbm['n_cb']>=15) & (cbm['n_ncb']>=50)].copy()
print(f"Cells with CB n>=15, nCB n>=50: {len(cbm)}")

div = np.zeros(len(cbm))
for name in TOP5.values():
    p_cb = cbm[f'{name}_cb'].values / cbm['n_cb'].values
    p_ncb = cbm[f'{name}_ncb'].values / cbm['n_ncb'].values
    div += np.abs(p_cb - p_ncb)
cbm['divergence'] = div / 2
print(f"Mean CB-vs-nCB cell divergence: {cbm['divergence'].mean():.4f}")
print(f"Median: {cbm['divergence'].median():.4f}")

top_cb_div = cbm.nlargest(20, 'divergence').copy()
top_cb_div['center_hex'] = top_cb_div['cell'].apply(cell_to_rgb_hex)
def winner_pair2(row):

    return max(cb_pcts, key=cb_pcts.get), cb_pcts[max(cb_pcts, key=cb_pcts.get)], max(ncb_pcts, key=ncb_pcts.get), ncb_pcts[max(ncb_pcts, key=ncb_pcts.get)]
wp = top_cb_div.apply(lambda r: pd.Series(winner_pair2(r), index=['cb_winner','cb_winner_pct','ncb_winner','ncb_winner_pct']), axis=1)
top_cb_div = pd.concat([top_cb_div, wp], axis=1)
print("\nTop 20 cells with highest CB-vs-non-CB naming divergence:")

top_cb_div.to_csv('/tmp/cb_divergent_cells.csv', index=False)

raw_evidence.label: Population colorblindness ratio benchmark mismatch
raw_evidence.content: Adjusted population estimates put red-green colorblindness at ~8% of XY individuals and ~0.5% of XX (a ~16x ratio). This suggests strong selection bias on both sides: XX users who are color-curious are more likely to self-report colorblindness (a soft form of color sensitivity), and many XY users with mild color vision deficiency may not consider themselves 'colorblind' for survey purposes. The implication for color-naming research: the xkcd colorblind subsample is substantially less colorblind, in absolute terms, than a true population sample would be — yet the naming differences observed in ana_19 are still robust.

raw_evidence.label: Chromosomal sex and color vision
raw_evidence.content: The dataset records, per user, whether they self-reported having a Y chromosome (a proxy for chromosomal sex) and whether they reported being colorblind. This framing — using chromosomes rather than gender — was deliberate: red-green color blindness is X-linked recessive, so individuals with one X chromosome (XY) are far more likely to be colorblind than those with two (XX). Population estimates put red-green color vision deficiency at about 8% of XY individuals versus 0.5% of XX individuals — roughly a 16x difference. Beyond physiology, the World Color Survey and follow-up linguistic research have documented that women use significantly more elaborate non-basic color terms (mauve, chartreuse, beige) and make finer green/blue distinctions, while men more often use the merged 'grue' category. The xkcd data is a chance to measure both effects in a single English-speaking online sample.

raw_evidence.label: Monitor calibration and display history
raw_evidence.content: In 2010, the survey took place during a major display transition. CRT monitors, which had dominated for decades, were being rapidly replaced by LCDs (and a small population of early LED-backlit units). The two technologies render color differently: CRTs use phosphors and have characteristic warm spots and gamma curves, while LCDs vary widely depending on panel type (TN, IPS, VA) and backlight. The xkcd survey asked respondents about their monitor type because the same RGB hex code can appear visibly different on different hardware — the survey's 'true' answer is necessarily an average over a heterogeneous viewing population. By 2010 roughly 90%+ of respondents reported LCDs and only ~6% reported CRTs.

raw_evidence.label: Monitor type: small but visible effect on pink/green balance
raw_evidence.content: Aggregate naming on LCDs vs CRTs shows a consistent pattern: LCD users say 'pink' 12.50% of the time vs CRT users 10.21% (a 2.29 pp gap), and CRT users say 'green' 32.67% vs LCD's 29.58% (3.09 pp). 'Brown' is also more common on CRTs (8.53% vs 7.13%). The signature: CRTs render colors slightly warmer/dimmer (phosphor characteristics), so pinks tend to read as reds or browns, greens look more saturated. The differences are smaller than chromosome differences but cleanly directional.

raw_evidence.label: Berlin & Kay basic color terms
raw_evidence.content: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay's 1969 study, expanded by the World Color Survey across 110 languages, established that human languages acquire basic color terms in a near-universal order: first black/white, then red, then green or yellow, then blue, then brown, then purple/pink/orange/grey. Modern English has the full eleven-term basic vocabulary (black, white, red, green, yellow, blue, brown, purple, pink, orange, grey). Anything beyond these is a 'hyponym' — a modified or derived term. The xkcd dataset lets us empirically rank how often each basic term and its hyponyms get used, and how the most popular non-basic colors (teal, lime, tan, beige) compete with basics for naming territory.

raw_evidence.label: Cultural afterlife of the xkcd palette
raw_evidence.content: The 954-color xkcd palette is now embedded across the design and data-science ecosystem. matplotlib ships it as the `xkcd:` color namespace (e.g. `xkcd:cerulean`). R, Julia, JavaScript, and Python design libraries all expose the same names. Web color pickers, design tools, and even some academic visualization papers reference 'xkcd cerulean' as a portable, reproducible color identifier. This means the survey's quirks — the over-representation of muted pastels in 'feminine' suggestions, the dominance of compound names like 'dusty teal', the absence of culturally specific names common in other languages — have been quietly baked into the visual culture of modern computing.

Purple's #1 ranking reflects ranking by *name uniqueness/distinctness* in the survey-cleaning algorithm, not by frequency.

raw_evidence.label: Berlin & Kay basic color terms
raw_evidence.content: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay's 1969 study, expanded by the World Color Survey across 110 languages, established that human languages acquire basic color terms in a near-universal order: first black/white, then red, then green or yellow, then blue, then brown, then purple/pink/orange/grey. Modern English has the full eleven-term basic vocabulary (black, white, red, green, yellow, blue, brown, purple, pink, orange, grey). Anything beyond these is a 'hyponym' — a modified or derived term. The xkcd dataset lets us empirically rank how often each basic term and its hyponyms get used, and how the most popular non-basic colors (teal, lime, tan, beige) compete with basics for naming territory.

sources.title: Basic Color Terms — Wikipedia
facts: Berlin & Kay 1969 proposed languages acquire color terms in a fixed order
English has 11 basic color terms
Order: black/white → red → green/yellow → blue → brown → purple/pink/orange/grey

raw_evidence.label: Cultural afterlife of the xkcd palette
raw_evidence.content: The 954-color xkcd palette is now embedded across the design and data-science ecosystem. matplotlib ships it as the `xkcd:` color namespace (e.g. `xkcd:cerulean`). R, Julia, JavaScript, and Python design libraries all expose the same names. Web color pickers, design tools, and even some academic visualization papers reference 'xkcd cerulean' as a portable, reproducible color identifier. This means the survey's quirks — the over-representation of muted pastels in 'feminine' suggestions, the dominance of compound names like 'dusty teal', the absence of culturally specific names common in other languages — have been quietly baked into the visual culture of modern computing.

Purple's #1 ranking reflects ranking by *name uniqueness/distinctness* in the survey-cleaning algorithm, not by frequency.

raw_evidence.label: Hue distribution of the 949 named colors
raw_evidence.content: Binning the 949 named hexes into 12 hue buckets reveals a strong English-language bias. Yellow (45-75°) tops the list with 152 named colors, followed by green (133), blue (126), and orange (119). The smallest chromatic bucket is purple (47 — the proper purple/violet wedge between blue and magenta) at less than a third of yellow's count. Eleven colors are achromatic (saturation <10%): black, white, six greys, charcoal, and silver. The skew reflects centuries-old vocabulary asymmetries — yellow has many sub-categories (gold, mustard, ochre, butter, lemon, banana, ...) while the saturated red/violet wedge is described mostly with shading modifiers.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_06 ===")
# bucket by hue (15-degree bins). Treat low-saturation (S<0.1) as 'achromatic'.
def hue_bucket(row):
    if row['S'] < 0.1:
        return 'achromatic (gray/white/black)'
    h = row['H']
    if h < 15 or h >= 345: return 'red (0-15, 345-360)'
    if h < 45: return 'orange (15-45)'
    if h < 75: return 'yellow (45-75)'
    if h < 105: return 'yellow-green (75-105)'
    if h < 165: return 'green (105-165)'
    if h < 195: return 'cyan/teal (165-195)'
    if h < 255: return 'blue (195-255)'
    if h < 285: return 'purple (255-285)'
    if h < 315: return 'magenta (285-315)'
    return 'pink (315-345)'

color_ranks['hue_bucket'] = color_ranks.apply(hue_bucket, axis=1)
hue_counts = color_ranks['hue_bucket'].value_counts()
print(hue_counts)
print(f"\nTotal: {len(color_ranks)}")

raw_evidence.label: Berlin & Kay basic color terms
raw_evidence.content: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay's 1969 study, expanded by the World Color Survey across 110 languages, established that human languages acquire basic color terms in a near-universal order: first black/white, then red, then green or yellow, then blue, then brown, then purple/pink/orange/grey. Anything beyond these is a 'hyponym' — a modified or derived term. The xkcd dataset lets us empirically rank how often each basic term and its hyponyms get used, and how the most popular non-basic colors (teal, lime, tan, beige) compete with basics for naming territory.

raw_evidence.label: Compound names — 72.5% are multi-word
raw_evidence.content: Only 261 of the 949 names (27.5%) are single words. 606 are two-word compounds (e.g. 'dusty teal'), 81 are three-word ('very pale blue'), and one outlier is six words ('purple/blue'). The most productive heads — the noun the modifier qualifies — are green (170 names end in 'green'), blue (110), pink (52), purple (47), and brown (44). Twelve colors end in '-ish' (e.g. 'greenish blue') and 25 single-word names end in '-y' (dusty, browny, etc). The data shows a robust pattern: English compounds colors compositionally, with green and blue acting as the most generative anchor categories.

raw_evidence.label: Berlin & Kay basic color terms
raw_evidence.content: Brent Berlin and Paul Kay's 1969 study, expanded by the World Color Survey across 110 languages, established that human languages acquire basic color terms in a near-universal order: first black/white, then red, then green or yellow, then blue, then brown, then purple/pink/orange/grey. Modern English has the full eleven-term basic vocabulary (black, white, red, green, yellow, blue, brown, purple, pink, orange, grey). Anything beyond these is a 'hyponym' — a modified or derived term. The xkcd dataset lets us empirically rank how often each basic term and its hyponyms get used, and how the most popular non-basic colors (teal, lime, tan, beige) compete with basics for naming territory.

raw_evidence.label: Cultural afterlife of the xkcd palette
raw_evidence.content: The 954-color xkcd palette is now embedded across the design and data-science ecosystem. matplotlib ships it as the `xkcd:` color namespace (e.g. `xkcd:cerulean`). R, Julia, JavaScript, and Python design libraries all expose the same names. Web color pickers, design tools, and even some academic visualization papers reference 'xkcd cerulean' as a portable, reproducible color identifier. This means the survey's quirks — the over-representation of muted pastels in 'feminine' suggestions, the dominance of compound names like 'dusty teal', the absence of culturally specific names common in other languages — have been quietly baked into the visual culture of modern computing.

Source: Linguistic relativity and the color naming debate — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linguistic_relativity_and_the_color_naming_debate) Facts: Russian speakers distinguish light and dark blue faster due to separate basic terms; Berlin & Kay supported a universalist account; later work documented relativist effects

raw_evidence.label: Why color naming is scientifically interesting
raw_evidence.content: Color is the textbook case for the Sapir-Whorf debate: does the language we speak shape how we perceive the world? Berlin and Kay's universalist account argued that color cognition is largely culture-independent. Later work showed that linguistic categories do measurably shift discrimination thresholds (Russian speakers, who have separate words for light and dark blue, distinguish them faster). The xkcd dataset operates within a single language but with massive within-language variation — letting us see where consensus is rock-solid (red, blue, green) and where it dissolves into a fog of competing terms (teal/turquoise/cyan; mauve/lilac/lavender/purple).

raw_evidence.label: Most canonical cells per name — perfect-agreement exemplars
raw_evidence.content: At the centers of each named region, agreement is essentially total. For 'green', cells like RGB (10,176,10) (#0aa00a) and (10,181,10) (#0ab50a) get 100% green among 1,400+ answers each. Pure 'blue' cells like #0aa0e0 and #208ae0 reach 100% blue (n=805 and 977). For 'purple', #602060 reaches 99.6% purple. The most canonical 'pink' cell (#f58a8a) achieves 99.9%. The cleanest 'brown' (#a04a0a) hits 100% brown over 801 answers. These are the prototypical exemplars — RGB triples that the entire English-speaking xkcd readership names identically.

raw_evidence.label: The most ambiguous cells — naming boundaries
raw_evidence.content: The 25 most ambiguous cells — winner share 33.9–50.8% — sit on the geometric boundaries between named regions. The single most contested cell, RGB ~(96,96,96) ('#606060', a true mid-grey), splits 33.9% purple, 25% brown, 23.2% blue, 16.1% green. Mid-grey gets *every* top-5 name: the brain has no anchor when nothing is saturated. Other contested cells include: '#b58a8a' (rose-grey: 35% purple / 32% pink / 31% brown), '#cab50a' (yellow-green: 45% green / 43% brown), and '#75f5ca' (cyan-green: 50% green / 49% blue). The list traces every border on the color wheel — the green/blue line at cyan, the blue/purple line at indigo, the pink/brown line at salmon, the purple/pink line at magenta.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_14 ===")
amb = ws.nsmallest(25, 'winner_pct').copy()
# convert center RGB to hex
def rgb_to_hex(r,g,b):
    return '#%02x%02x%02x' % (int(r),int(g),int(b))
amb['center_hex'] = amb.apply(lambda r: rgb_to_hex(r['cR'],r['cG'],r['cB']), axis=1)
print("Top 25 most ambiguous cells (closest to a naming boundary):")
print(amb[['center_hex','n','winner','winner_pct','purple','green','blue','pink','brown']].to_string(index=False))
amb.to_csv('/tmp/most_ambiguous_cells.csv', index=False)

# Save full well-sampled set
ws['center_hex'] = ws.apply(lambda r: rgb_to_hex(r['cR'],r['cG'],r['cB']), axis=1)
ws.to_csv('/tmp/well_sampled_cells.csv', index=False)

raw_evidence.label: Why color naming is scientifically interesting
raw_evidence.content: Color is the textbook case for the Sapir-Whorf debate: does the language we speak shape how we perceive the world? Berlin and Kay's universalist account argued that color cognition is largely culture-independent. Later work showed that linguistic categories do measurably shift discrimination thresholds (Russian speakers, who have separate words for light and dark blue, distinguish them faster). The xkcd dataset operates within a single language but with massive within-language variation — letting us see where consensus is rock-solid (red, blue, green) and where it dissolves into a fog of competing terms (teal/turquoise/cyan; mauve/lilac/lavender/purple).

raw_evidence.label: Most canonical cells per name — perfect-agreement exemplars
raw_evidence.content: At the centers of each named region, agreement is essentially total. For 'green', cells like RGB (10,176,10) (#0aa00a) and (10,181,10) (#0ab50a) get 100% green among 1,400+ answers each. Pure 'blue' cells like #0aa0e0 and #208ae0 reach 100% blue (n=805 and 977). For 'purple', #602060 reaches 99.6% purple. The most canonical 'pink' cell (#f58a8a) achieves 99.9%. The cleanest 'brown' (#a04a0a) hits 100% brown over 801 answers. These are the prototypical exemplars — RGB triples that the entire English-speaking xkcd readership names identically.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_15 ===")
for name in TOP5.values():
    pure = ws[ws['winner']==name].nlargest(5, 'winner_pct')
    pure['center_hex'] = pure.apply(lambda r: rgb_to_hex(r['cR'],r['cG'],r['cB']), axis=1)
    print(f"\nMost canonically '{name}' cells (highest winner_pct):")
    print(pure[['center_hex','n','winner_pct',name]].to_string(index=False))

raw_evidence.label: The most ambiguous cells — naming boundaries
raw_evidence.content: The 25 most ambiguous cells — winner share 33.9–50.8% — sit on the geometric boundaries between named regions. The single most contested cell, RGB ~(96,96,96) ('#606060', a true mid-grey), splits 33.9% purple, 25% brown, 23.2% blue, 16.1% green. Mid-grey gets *every* top-5 name: the brain has no anchor when nothing is saturated. Other contested cells include: '#b58a8a' (rose-grey: 35% purple / 32% pink / 31% brown), '#cab50a' (yellow-green: 45% green / 43% brown), and '#75f5ca' (cyan-green: 50% green / 49% blue). The list traces every border on the color wheel — the green/blue line at cyan, the blue/purple line at indigo, the pink/brown line at salmon, the purple/pink line at magenta.
